title: Acme Bank - Security review (KMS integration, rotation, audit evidence)
topics: Customer-managed KMS/HSM envelope encryption model (KEK/DEK) and where keys live
Supported KMS providers in Private deployments (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS patterns)
Rotation cadence expectations (quarterly vs annual) and Redwood operational steps
Dual-read / dual-decrypt window and cutover flags
Audit evidence: what artifacts exist, what can be exported, and who approves
Failure modes: KMS outage/throttling/AccessDenied/wrong key ID; circuit breaker and retry budgets
Logging/telemetry: metrics, traces, dashboards, alerting and on-call runbooks
Least-privilege IAM roles and break-glass access
summary: Acme Bank security team reviewed Redwood Inference’s customer-managed KMS integration for Private deployments, focusing on envelope encryption, rotation workflow (including dual-decrypt window and rollback), and what audit evidence Redwood can provide. Acme emphasized quarterly rotation, segregation of duties, and clear behavior during KMS degradation/outage. Redwood committed to sharing the Private KMS operator guide, rotation procedure/evidence checklist, and a sample audit-log export schema including rotation events, plus scheduling a follow-up deep dive on failure-mode behavior and operational runbooks.
questions: Can Redwood support quarterly rotation without downtime, and what is the rollback procedure if decrypt errors spike?
During a KMS outage, do you fail closed or can you continue using cached materials? What is the blast radius and what telemetry exists?
What artifacts do you provide for audits (SOC2/ISO narratives, approval evidence, timestamps, log exports)?
How do you ensure least privilege (separate principals for runtime decrypt vs rotation actions)?
How do you detect and surface permission misconfigurations (AccessDenied) in a way operators can act on quickly?

Schedule a 45-min technical deep dive focused on failure-mode behavior (timeouts/throttling/outage) and operational runbooks.

transcript:
Meeting: Acme Bank - Security review (KMS integration, rotation, audit evidence)
Date: 2025-11-06
Recorded: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes

Attendees (Redwood): Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Ethan Park, Allison Grant, Kira Thompson
Attendees (Acme Bank): Sarah Klein, Raj Patel, Megan O’Connor, Tom Nguyen, Irene Wu

---

[00:00] Marcus Lin: Alright, I think we’re live. Thanks everyone for making time. I’m Marcus, I run security engineering at Redwood Inference. On with me are Kevin, Ethan, Allison, and Kira.

[00:11] Sarah Klein: Great. Thanks Marcus. This is Sarah, cloud security. Raj is our principal architect. Megan from GRC, Tom from platform, and Irene from SecOps.

[00:21] Marcus Lin: Perfect. The agenda we got from Naomi— uh sorry, from our PM— was KMS integration, rotation cadence, audit evidence, and then failure mode behavior. We can go wherever you want.

[00:35] Megan O’Connor: Yeah that’s right. We’re trying to close out third-party risk items. We need to understand: who holds keys, how rotations happen, and what proof we get.

[00:44] Raj Patel: And very specifically, we’ve been burned by systems that say “customer managed keys” but then rotation is like a ticket to the vendor and two weeks later someone flips a switch. So we want the mechanics.

[00:56] Marcus Lin: Understood. Let’s start with the model. For Private deployments, the customer owns the KMS. We do envelope encryption: a KEK in your KMS wraps DEKs that encrypt data at rest. Redwood services request decrypt/encrypt from KMS as needed; we do not store plaintext master keys.

[01:15] Tom Nguyen: When you say “data at rest,” what data are we talking? Prompts? Logs? KV cache? Like, what’s actually encrypted with that DEK?

[01:24] Ethan Park: Good question. In Private, it’s primarily persisted control-plane secrets and any persisted customer configuration secrets. For app payloads, it depends on the customer’s logging settings; our recommendation is to not persist prompts by default. KV cache is memory, not at rest.

[01:40] Sarah Klein: Do you encrypt tokens / completions in logs if we enable request logging for debugging?

[01:45] Marcus Lin: If you opt into payload logging, yes, the storage layer uses envelope encryption. But we also encourage redaction and sampling. Kira can send the operator guide section where that’s defined.

[01:56] Kira Thompson: Yep, there’s a “Data handling + logging” section in the Private KMS guide with defaults and toggles.

[02:02] Raj Patel: KMS providers. We’re mostly AWS, but we do have some Azure workloads. Is it one and done, or do you support multi-cloud key backends?

[02:11] Ethan Park: In Private, it’s “choose your backend per deployment.” The patterns are AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault (including HSM tier), and GCP Cloud KMS. The integration is through a standardized client wrapper that handles timeouts, retry budgets, and error mapping. We don’t do cross-cloud “one deployment uses two KMS backends” today.

[02:34] Sarah Klein: That’s okay. Our likely path is AWS first.

[02:37] Megan O’Connor: Rotation cadence: we do quarterly for high-risk systems. Can you support that, and what evidence do we get?

[02:46] Kevin Osei: Yes. Mechanically, we treat key rotation as key versioning: you introduce a new key version / new KEK alias target, then there’s a dual-decrypt window where systems can decrypt old and new, then you cut over encryption to the new key version, and then you eventually retire the old.

[03:08] Raj Patel: Dual decrypt is the piece that matters. How long is that window and who controls it?

[03:13] Ethan Park: It’s configurable. For Private, we expect the customer to control when to start and end the window via config flags in the control plane (or via the installer if that’s the interface you prefer). Default is conservative: dual-decrypt is enabled for a short period during the cutover, then disabled once verification passes.

[03:33] Tom Nguyen: What does verification mean? Like checksums? Or just “no errors”?

[03:38] Ethan Park: More “no decrypt errors and no mismatch signals.” We track decrypt failure rate by error taxonomy— AccessDenied, NotFound, Throttling, Timeout, InvalidCiphertext. During cutover, you set a success criteria: error rate stays below X, latency stays within bounds, and no “invalid ciphertext” type spikes. If it does, rollback is: re-enable decrypt with old version and revert encryption to old until the issue is identified.

[04:08] Irene Wu: When you say “mismatch signals,” is there a case where decrypt returns something wrong, not just an error?

[04:14] Kevin Osei: Practically, KMS decrypt is either success or error, but we’ve seen “wrong key id configured” and data that was encrypted under a different key. That shows up as InvalidCiphertext. We treat that as a strong signal to stop and roll back.

[04:30] Raj Patel: Ok. But during a KMS outage, what do you do? Fail closed or try to keep serving? Our policy is generally fail closed for decrypt, but we also can’t take an outage on critical apps.

[04:43] Marcus Lin: We split it by operation and data sensitivity. For anything that requires decrypting persisted secrets, we fail closed. For “read path” operations that can proceed without decrypt, we continue. We also have caching for some key metadata but not “skip encryption.”

[05:02] Raj Patel: Do you cache decrypted data keys?

[05:05] Ethan Park: Limited and bounded. There is an in-memory cache for recently used wrapped DEKs to reduce KMS calls, but it’s keyed to the key version and has TTLs. We do not persist decrypted DEKs to disk. And we have guardrails to avoid stale material across rotations.

[05:25] Sarah Klein: I’m going to be picky: “recently used wrapped DEKs” is still a key. Are you saying you cache the plaintext DEK?

[05:32] Ethan Park: Sorry, yeah, the plaintext DEK exists in memory during use; the cache is effectively an in-memory reuse window so you’re not calling KMS for every operation. The TTL is short, and it’s bounded by process lifetime. We can provide the exact default TTL and the override policy.

[05:53] Raj Patel: That’s the critical detail. We’ll need that documented.

[05:56] Kira Thompson: It’s in the operator guide, but I’ll double check it’s explicit. We’ve had feedback that it was too hand-wavy.

[06:05] Allison Grant: And from an observability side, we emit metrics for KMS call rates so you can see if caching is effective or if you’re thrashing KMS.

[06:13] Megan O’Connor: For audit evidence: we need change management artifacts. Who requested rotation, who approved, when it was executed, what key identifiers were involved, and then logs proving it occurred.

[06:28] Kevin Osei: We can support that. We have rotation-related audit log events: “key version updated,” “cutover flag toggled,” “dual decrypt enabled/disabled,” and those can be exported via the audit log exporter for SIEM ingestion. In Private, you can also rely on your cloud provider logs (e.g., CloudTrail for KMS API calls) as additional evidence.

[06:53] Megan O’Connor: Do you provide a template? Like a checklist our auditors can sign?

[06:58] Kevin Osei: Yes— we have an evidence checklist template. It includes fields for the ticket ID, approver names, timestamps, and pointers to exported audit events and KMS logs. It’s designed to be SOC 2 / ISO friendly.

[07:15] Raj Patel: On approvals: do you require Redwood approval to rotate, or can we do it ourselves?

[07:20] Marcus Lin: In Private, you can do it yourself. Redwood can assist, but it’s not a vendor-controlled change. We recommend segregating duties: one principal performs the rotation actions, another approves. The least-privilege IAM roles we provide reflect that separation.

[07:38] Sarah Klein: That’s good. We have strict IAM requirements: no wildcards, scoped ARNs, region restrictions. Can your Terraform modules handle that?

[07:47] Ethan Park: Our baseline policies are least privilege. We can scope to specific key ARNs and specific operations: Decrypt/Encrypt for runtime role; and separate role for rotation actions like UpdateAlias, DescribeKey, etc. The exact verbs vary by cloud.

[08:04] Tom Nguyen: We also require break-glass with time-bound access. How do you handle that operationally?

[08:11] Marcus Lin: Break-glass for our team is mostly relevant in Hosted/Dedicated. In Private, your org controls access, so you can enforce time-bound roles on your side. For Redwood personnel access, it’s “no default access,” and any emergency access is time-bound and requires approvals. But for Private we usually don’t need access if you’re running it.

[08:34] Irene Wu: Failures. Let’s talk about KMS throttling. We’ve seen systems melt themselves by retrying.

[08:41] Allison Grant: Yep. We’ve put in explicit retry budgets with backoff and jitter, and we add a circuit breaker so when KMS is failing, services don’t stampede it. We alert on error rate by error code and on p95/p99 latency for KMS calls.

[08:58] Raj Patel: Circuit breaker means what? You stop calling KMS after N failures?

[09:03] Allison Grant: Essentially. There’s a threshold and a cool-down. During open breaker, you avoid immediate retries and you surface a clear error upstream. The goal is to prevent cascading failures and protect KMS quota.

[09:18] Sarah Klein: But then you’re failing requests.

[09:21] Marcus Lin: Correct— but it’s controlled failure rather than a full system collapse. For decrypt-dependent operations, it’s safer to fail and page than to partially succeed with inconsistent state.

[09:35] Megan O’Connor: We need that documented, “availability vs cryptographic strictness.” Our auditors ask “can you operate without KMS.”

[09:43] Marcus Lin: We can document it as: KMS is a hard dependency for decrypting protected persisted data. We do not bypass KMS for decrypt. For transient requests, we can continue to serve as long as we don’t need to touch encrypted storage.

[10:02] Raj Patel: What about startup? If KMS is down during pod start, do you crash loop?

[10:08] Ethan Park: Depends on the component. Control plane services that require decrypting secrets at startup will fail readiness and not serve. There’s also preflight checks in the installer so you detect permissions and key configuration before you get into a crash loop.

[10:23] Tom Nguyen: Preflight checks would be huge. We want to validate key ID and permissions before rollout.

[10:29] Kira Thompson: The installer validation generates a report you can keep as evidence too. It shows which API calls succeeded and what principal was used.

[10:40] Sarah Klein: Nice.

[10:42] Raj Patel: Another failure: wrong key ARN configured. Does it show up as NotFound or AccessDenied? And do you surface something actionable?

[10:51] Kevin Osei: We map those into a canonical taxonomy. AccessDenied is separate from NotFound. We also attach remediation hints in the logs like “missing kms:Decrypt on key ARN X for role Y.” Some of that is provider-specific but we try to be explicit.

[11:12] Irene Wu: Can those errors be routed to our SIEM? We want alerts when AccessDenied appears.

[11:18] Allison Grant: Yes— metrics have tags for environment/region/service/error_category, and logs include a consistent field for “kms.error_category” and “kms.key_id” (redacted or hashed depending on settings). In Private you can ship logs to your system.

[11:37] Raj Patel: Wait, you said “key id redacted.” We usually want the full ARN for triage.

[11:42] Marcus Lin: In Private you can configure that. Default is to avoid leaking key identifiers into multi-tenant logs, but in Private it’s your environment. We can recommend best practices.

[11:57] Megan O’Connor: Switching gears: rotation proof. We often need to show that rotation occurred within policy. So we need timestamps and what changed.

[12:07] Kevin Osei: That’s what the audit events provide. Example event: “kms_rotation.cutover_enabled” with actor, timestamp, previous value, new value, and correlating change ticket ID if you include it.

[12:24] Megan O’Connor: Good. Also, do you align this to SOC 2 CC6/CC7, ISO 27001 controls? I need a narrative.

[12:34] Marcus Lin: Yes. We can provide a short narrative mapping: key management, change management, logging and monitoring. But for Private, you’ll also have shared responsibility language.

[12:48] Sarah Klein: Raj, anything else on crypto side?

[12:51] Raj Patel: Yes. Key rotation: do you support “automatic rotation” via KMS native rotation, or do you require manual version pinning?

[13:01] Ethan Park: We support both patterns, but we prefer explicit versioning / alias cutover for predictability. Native automatic rotation can change underlying key material without an explicit cutover event from our control plane. If you use native rotation, we still recommend an explicit application-level rotation process for wrapped DEKs.

[13:27] Raj Patel: So “KMS rotates the KEK” doesn’t automatically rewrap DEKs.

[13:30] Ethan Park: Exactly. That’s a common misunderstanding. We can do scheduled rewrap jobs as part of the runbook.

[13:41] Tom Nguyen: Does that mean a big data rewrite? Like re-encrypting everything?

[13:46] Ethan Park: It can be incremental. You can rewrap DEKs without rewriting the entire encrypted payload, depending on the storage format. For most of our persisted secrets/config, it’s manageable and done in the background with throttling.

[14:03] Sarah Klein: Ok.

[14:05] Irene Wu: Game days. Do you test KMS outage scenarios?

[14:10] Allison Grant: Yes, we do KMS outage/throttling game days in staging. We inject timeouts and throttling, verify circuit breaker behavior, dashboards, and paging. We can share the high-level results and what we fixed.

[14:28] Raj Patel: Please share. That helps us.

[14:31] Megan O’Connor: Also: retention. How long do you keep audit logs?

[14:37] Kevin Osei: In Private, you control log retention because it’s in your environment. Our exporter supports sending events to your SIEM. We’ll document required retention for compliance and how to configure it.

[14:52] Sarah Klein: Quick check: this is Private deployment only, right? We’re not going hosted.

[14:56] Marcus Lin: Correct, we’re discussing Private. But the concepts apply across modes.

[15:03] Tom Nguyen: One more: data-plane runtime calls. Does the model runtime call KMS on every request?

[15:10] Ethan Park: Typically no. KMS is for persisted secrets and encryption keys, not per-token inference. If you’re storing something like an API credential for upstream, that’s decrypted at runtime when needed, but not per token. And caching reduces repeated calls.

[15:30] Raj Patel: That’s important. We want to avoid KMS as a hot path for inference.

[15:34] Marcus Lin: Same. Our design is not to put KMS on the per-token hot path.

[15:40] Sarah Klein: Alright. I think we covered the big rocks. Megan, anything else you need?

[15:46] Megan O’Connor: I need: the operator guide, the rotation runbook and evidence template, and sample audit log fields. And then we’ll send you our evidence checklist. Also if you can articulate the failure behavior in one page, that’s helpful.

[16:03] Kira Thompson: I can send the docs link and also a PDF export if you prefer. And we can add a “Failure mode behavior” appendix.

[16:12] Allison Grant: I’ll include dashboard screenshots and alert thresholds, plus what tags we use.

[16:18] Raj Patel: And I want the exact TTLs for in-memory key caching, and whether it’s configurable.

[16:24] Ethan Park: Yep. I’ll follow up with the defaults and recommended ranges, and where it’s enforced.

[16:31] Sarah Klein: Great. Next call: I’d like a technical deep dive with Raj and Tom with your engineers— maybe include the person who owns the installer validation too.

[16:41] Marcus Lin: Sounds good. Let’s do a 45-minute deep dive next week. We’ll bring the right folks.

[16:48] Megan O’Connor: And timeline: we need materials by mid next week for our risk committee.

[16:55] Kevin Osei: Understood. We’ll target Friday for the first set, then Tuesday for the dashboards/TTL details.

[17:03] Marcus Lin: Cool. Anything else before we wrap?

[17:06] Irene Wu: Just one: escalation path. If we have decrypt failures in production, who do we call?

[17:12] Marcus Lin: In Private, your on-call owns the infra, but we provide a runbook and you can engage Redwood support with a defined escalation to security/platform. We’ll include the escalation matrix in the doc pack.

[17:28] Sarah Klein: Ok, thanks everyone.

[17:31] Marcus Lin: Thanks all. We’ll follow up in email with links and scheduling.

---

Post-call notes (auto-generated):
- Acme emphasized quarterly rotation, segregation of duties, and evidence completeness (approvals + timestamps + exportable logs).
- Redwood to provide documentation pack and schedule deeper technical session on failure modes and operational controls.
